* perf(g): update animation promises once per frame (#2265)

* perf(g): update animation promises once per frame

Every animation started in a task queued its own no-op frame callback
(AnimationTimeline.tick, and restart() when seeking), and the timeline
wrapped each frame callback in two calls to updateAnimationsPromises,
which goes over every animation with promises. Starting N animations
in one task (G6 does this on every animated draw) therefore cost about
2·N² updatePromises calls in the next frame: 32 million for N = 4000.

Run updateAnimationsPromises once before and once after the frame's
callbacks instead. Nothing can change promise state between two
callbacks of the same frame, so the extra calls did nothing.

Tests: six traces of when ready/finished settle relative to frames and
playState, recorded on 6.3.1 and unchanged; three tests that the
bookkeeping stays linear when starting, or seeking paused or finished,
animations in one task (6.3.1: ~2 million calls for n = 1000).

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* test(g): assert the finished read in the promise scaling tests

The helper read `animation.finished` only for its side effect (it puts
the animation on the timeline's promise list), which CodeQL reports as
an expression with no effect. Assert on it instead.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Co-authored-by: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(web-animations-api): use bezier-easing 3.2 closed-form solver (#2256)

Replace the sample table + Newton-Raphson + bisection search with the
closed-form solver of bezier-easing 3.2: exact (~1e-14 instead of up to
~1e-3), no backward jump on steep curves such as (1, 0, 0, 1).

Progress outside [0, 1] now saturates to 0 / 1 instead of going through
the old search, which returned arbitrary values there.

Co-authored-by: hustcc <i@hust.cc>
